name: Teleportation Circles Ruin Non-Living Cargo
description: Passing through a teleportation circle is hard on anything that isn't alive. Non-living matter carried through — goods, coin, raw materials, equipment not worn or wielded by a living creature making the trip — arrives damaged, spoiled, or destroyed outright, at the DM's discretion based on the material and the trip. Living creatures, and anything a living creature is wearing or wielding on their person, are unaffected. This is why teleportation circles are never used to move cargo directly.
notes: Explains why established trade (Long Arm Trading, the Yetgrese-Kaemahz crossing runs, etc.) still relies on ships and mundane transport instead of teleportation circles, even in a setting where circles exist and are used for people. A party that teleports often and needs to bring goods along should carry them inside a Bag of Holding (see the Bag of Holding Capacity house rule) — the contents of an extradimensional space aren't 'non-living cargo' being carried through in the normal sense, they're unaffected.

name: Bag of Holding Capacity
description: A Bag of Holding holds roughly 15 items of average size (that is, no larger than a backpack could reasonably hold on its own) rather than an effectively unlimited amount. It is a convenient way to carry a party's own gear and modest amounts of loot, not a substitute for a cargo hold — it cannot hold commercial-scale quantities of goods.
notes: Real 5e RAW technically caps a Bag of Holding by weight (500 lb) and volume (64 cubic feet) rather than item count, which in practice lets a creative player treat it as a small cargo hold. This house rule caps it by a rough item count instead, closer to 'a large adventurer's pack,' specifically so it can't be used to route around the Teleportation Circles Ruin Non-Living Cargo rule for anything beyond personal gear.

name: Crossing Profit System
description:
Governs profit/loss for ships running cargo between Yetgrese and Kaemahz. Roll 1d20 every week; the result is that week's outcome band, resolved to a gold value per the table below. Two consecutive weekly rolls make one 2-week cycle: the first week's gold value is kept as an unpaid intermediate result, and at the end of the second week the two values are added together — that combined total is what actually pays out (or is owed) to the party's finances. Ships engaged in this run generate no other income while doing so.

WEEKLY ROLL TABLE (1d20):
1 — Disaster. Roll 1d6 for severity, each entry is that week's gold value: 1-2 cargo spoiled/lost overboard (-500g), 3-4 cargo destroyed outright (-1,000g), 5 ship damaged badly, needs repair (-1,500g), 6 'or worse' — a genuine crisis (piracy, magical storm, crew lost) the DM should develop as a story beat, still -1,500g for accounting purposes.
2-5 — Bad week. Reduced but still positive profit: roll or pick 200g to 1,200g.
6-14 — Normal. Standard baseline profit: roll or pick 1,500g to 2,500g.
15-19 — Good week. Above-average: roll or pick 2,800g to 4,200g.
20 — Exceptional. Major profit spike or a valuable discovery: roll or pick 8,000g to 9,500g.

Worst possible 2-week result: Disaster+Disaster at worst severity both weeks, -1,500g + -1,500g = -3,000g. Best possible: Exceptional+Exceptional at the top of its range both weeks, 9,500g + 9,500g = 19,000g. Typical result (Normal both weeks, the single most likely specific outcome): roughly 3,000-5,000g, averaging about 4,000g every two weeks — the spikes in either direction are meant to be rare and dramatic, not the norm.
notes: The exact gold ranges per band are a homebrew design pass filling in numbers the project owner didn't specify beyond the outcome bands themselves and the three stated targets (worst case ~-3,000g, best case ~+19,000g, typical ~4,000g/2 weeks) — the ranges were built to hit those targets exactly at the extremes while keeping Normal+Normal as the realistic modal result. Adjust the specific gold figures freely if actual play doesn't match the intended feel. As of 2026-09-03, three ships are running this route until the project owner decides to stop it: Gilt Blades, Argent Sunrise, and Tilawam Sky. Not yet wired into any UI (the Weekly Events tool's existing income table only supports flat per-week min/max ranges, not this banded/two-week-combine structure) — for now this is a DM-executed-by-hand system, same as any other house rule; a real automated version would be a separate, larger build to ask for specifically.

name: Critical Hits
description: On a critical hit, double the total damage of the attack after all modifiers are applied, rather than doubling the damage dice only.
notes: Implemented because crits don't feel rewarding or powerful.

name: Critical Fail on Saving Throws
description: A natural 1 on a saving throw results in double damage taken, rather than just a failed save.
notes: Applies to both enemy and player saving throws for consistency.

name: Critical Roll Consequences
description: A natural 1 or natural 20 carries an additional consequence beyond automatic failure or success, at the DM's discretion. On a critical 1 attack roll, the attacker typically disarms themselves. On a critical 20, the consequence is a dramatic positive outcome suited to the moment — not just a hit, but something memorable. The nature of the consequence should fit the fiction and scale with the stakes.
notes: Keeps the extremes of the dice meaningful and dramatic in both directions. The DM has full latitude to interpret the consequence; consistency matters more than strict rules.

name: Stealth Awareness
description: While Hidden, a character gains advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks to notice hidden creatures or objects, and on Intelligence (Investigation) checks to find traps.
notes: From Solasta. Moving carefully and quietly also means moving attentively. Rewards players who choose stealth as a playstyle beyond just avoiding detection.

name: Spell Material Components
description: Material components (M) are not required to cast spells. In their place, spellcasters may use Weave Dust — a fine crystalline powder that serves as a universal substitute for all material components. Weave Dust can be purchased from alchemists, magic shops, and certain temples, or produced by breaking down traditional spell components or certain animal parts through a distillation process. The spell's original material cost roughly dictates how much dust is required. Dust is stored in small capsules, almost excluisvely made of silver, that hold enough for a simple spell. Weave Dust is sold in small vials and larger pouches; exact pricing varies by region but is generally 'per capsule'.
notes: Introduced to streamline play. Hunting for obscure specific components is more friction than fun at this table. Characters must still buy or otherwise procure the powder..

name: Weave Dust from Broken-Down Magic Items
description: A magic item can be destroyed and broken down into Weave Dust instead of sold for gold. The yield is calculated, not chosen freely: base = floor(item's recorded value_gp / 15). If the item has charges, apply a penalty for any missing at the time of destruction (missing_fraction = 1 - charges_current/charges_max): a rest-recharging item (regains charges on a long/short rest at no cost) has its base reduced by up to 30% at missing_fraction 1.0 (base *= 1 - 0.30*missing_fraction); a material-recharging item (needs a consumed material — a gem, rare reagent, etc. — to recharge) takes the same 30% reduction AND has the gp-equivalent cost of the missing charges' materials subtracted directly (converted at the same 15gp-per-dust rate). Finally, roll a d20 to add texture to the result: a 20 doubles the adjusted base, a 1 halves it, and any other roll shifts the value by a percentage equal to how far the roll sits from the 10/11 midpoint — roll 10 is -1%, roll 11 is +1%, roll 2 is -9%, roll 19 is +9%, and so on one percentage point per step. Round the final result down. This is a one-time calculation performed at the moment of destruction, not a recurring cost.
notes: Extends the Spell Material Components house rule's existing 'produced by breaking down... certain animal parts' framing to magic items specifically — same in-fiction distillation process, applied to something with more stored magical potential than a spell component pouch. Requires every magic item to carry a real, once-recorded value_gp at authoring time (found by matching it to an identical or very similar real item's published price — this also just makes selling items for gold more grounded, not only dust) rather than deriving a price from rarity alone, since a bare rarity band can't distinguish two items of the same rarity from each other. Charged items also need a recorded charges_recharge_type ('rest' or 'material') and, for material-recharging items, a per-charge material cost — filled in once, same as value_gp, not looked up repeatedly. Implemented as CharacterInventory.vue's item-delete dialog: choosing to destroy for dust auto-rolls and shows the result rather than requiring the DM to do this math by hand, with the usual delete confirmation guarding against an accidental destroy.

name: Caster Prestidigitation
description: All arcane and divine casters receive a free, flavor-appropriate form of Prestidigitation that does not count against their spell allotment. Sorcerers and Wizards receive standard Prestidigitation. Druids receive standard Druidcraft. Clerics receive Divine Prestidigitation (a divine-flavored equivalent). Warlocks receive Dark Prestidigitation (a patron-flavored equivalent that does not draw from the Weave). These spells are always prepared and cannot be removed.
notes: Casters should feel like casters without spending a cantrip slot on it. Mages wave their hand and make a small change in the world; druids make a flower bloom. These spells are the mechanical expression of that identity.

name: Crowd
description: Up to 5 weak or narratively uninteresting creatures can be merged into a single Crowd, tracked and acting as one creature instead of several separate stat blocks. A Crowd's Strength rating starts equal to the number of creatures merged into it (n, up to 5) and represents how many of them are still meaningfully fighting. Pool their hit points into one total for the Crowd. Strength is the current HP's position among n even thresholds of the Crowd's max HP, rounded up — for a Crowd of 5 with 50 max HP, Strength stays at 5 until HP drops to 40 or below, then drops to 4 until HP reaches 30 or below, then 3 until 20 or below, then 2 until 10 or below, then 1 until the Crowd is destroyed at 0 HP. Set the Crowd's AC in line with the AC of the creatures that formed it, and give it 1-3 special abilities flavored to whatever those creatures were. The Crowd moves as a single unit, and any condition that affects it affects the whole group at once — no per-member tracking. Two ways to scale the Crowd's offense down as Strength drops — pick whichever fits the specific Crowd (or the table's general preference) rather than mixing both on the same Crowd: (1) the Crowd has Strength-many attacks, extra attacks, and bonus-action attacks, so the number of attacks shrinks as Strength drops; or (2) the Crowd always takes one action, one bonus action, and its normal Extra Attack as if at full strength, and instead the damage or severity of each attack shrinks with Strength. Area-of-effect saving throws against a Crowd always succeed — it's an abstraction, not an individual rolling its own save — but the damage isn't just the normal halved amount: take the save-succeeded (halved) damage and multiply it by the Crowd's current Strength before applying it. Example: a Crowd formed from 5 creatures with 50 max HP, currently at 30 HP (Strength 3), is hit by a fireball that would deal 20 damage — halved for the successful save is 10, multiplied by Strength 3 is 30, which exactly destroys the Crowd.
notes: Homebrew abstraction for running a pack of mooks (goblins, guards, rats, etc.) as one tracked unit instead of five separate stat blocks. Named 'Crowd' rather than 'Swarm' since Swarm is already a real, distinct D&D creature type/rules concept ('Cluster' was the other name considered). The attack-scaling approach (fewer attacks vs. weaker attacks) is a deliberate open choice, not a settled default — decide per Crowd. Not yet wired into the Combat tracker UI (Battle.vue/CombatContext.vue) — see TODO.md.

name: Attuned Stone Backlash
description: Whenever the bearer of the Stone of the Rootbound Ward or the Stone of the Broken Vein uses one of the stone's active abilities — including the shared combo ability The Stones Agree — the bearer must succeed on a DC 12 Constitution saving throw or take 1d6 damage: feedback from channeling power they were never actually trained to hold. Does not apply to the stones' passive tremorsense, since standing near ground the stone already senses isn't 'using' anything.
notes: Applies per-use, per-bearer. When both bearers trigger The Stones Agree together, each makes their own separate backlash save.
